name: Cavity prevention & decay
description: Understand what happens beneath the surface, and give your everyday routine a clear purpose.
keywords: How decay starts Bacteria use sugars and starches to produce acids that remove minerals from enamel. Repeated exposure can lead to a cavity. Early decay may have no symptoms. Early changes vs. a cavity A white spot can signal early mineral loss. Saliva and fluoride can help repair enamel before a hole forms. Once a cavity develops, a dentist usually restores the damaged tooth with a filling. Your everyday foundations Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth, and limit frequent sugary snacks and drinks. Keep regular dental visits and ask whether you would benefit from additional fluoride or sealants. When to book a visit Arrange a dental assessment for tooth pain or sensitivity. Tell your dental team about persistent dry mouth and any changes you notice.

name: Get to know your gums
description: A simple guide to gum inflammation, periodontal disease, and the care that comes next.
keywords: Notice the early signs Swelling, tenderness, bleeding, persistent bad breath, or gums pulling away from teeth can signal a problem. Plaque can harden into tartar, which requires professional removal. Gingivitis: inflammation at the gumline Early gum disease can often improve with consistent brushing, cleaning between teeth, and professional care. Ask your dental team to demonstrate a technique that works for you. Periodontitis: deeper support is affected Disease can damage the tissues and bone supporting teeth. Treatment may include scaling and root planing, medication, or surgery. Your care and follow-up schedule depend on your needs. What your dental team checks An examination may include gum-pocket measurements, your medical history, and X-rays to assess bone support. A single measurement alone is not a complete diagnosis. Loose teeth or pain when chewing should be assessed.

name: A healthier smile. A healthier you.
description: Oral health is part of whole-person care. Here is how to understand the connections without the alarm.
keywords: What the research tells us Researchers study links between gum disease and conditions including cardiovascular disease and pregnancy complications. Shared risk factors and inflammation may help explain these associations. Evidence of an association does not establish that dental treatment prevents those other conditions. Diabetes and your mouth Diabetes raises the likelihood of gum disease and may slow healing. Gum disease can also make blood sugar harder to manage. Share your diabetes history with your dental team and continue the care plan from your medical team. Keep your care team connected Bring an up-to-date medication list and tell your dental team about health changes, pregnancy, and ongoing treatment. Ask how these may affect your oral care. Focus on what you can do Use your appointments to discuss symptoms and build a routine you can maintain. Dental care supports your oral health; it does not replace medical treatment.

name: More than a cleaning
description: Meet the prevention, assessment, and education behind a dental hygienist’s work.
keywords: Assess and understand Hygienists assess oral health, look for signs of disease, take dental X-rays, and share findings with the dentist. They document care so the team can follow changes over time. Clean and protect Removing plaque, tartar, and stains is part of preventive care. Hygienists may also apply fluoride or sealants to help protect teeth. Permitted services and supervision requirements vary by state and setting. Make home care practical Your hygienist can demonstrate brushing and cleaning between teeth, discuss diet, and help you choose oral care tools. Bring questions about what feels difficult in your routine. Make the most of your visit Write down your questions before the appointment. Ask what the findings mean, which habit to focus on first, and when your next visit should be.
